claims.claim: The right-to-repair debate is often framed primarily as a dispute over access to parts.
Manufacturers that withhold service information as intellectual property state that protecting creative work is a reason for doing so.
Intellectual-property protections can protect a repair manual's original expression without treating every useful fact about the machine as a protected company secret.
Repair manuals may contain expressive writing.
Connector locations, error codes, and test values commonly form the practical core of repair manuals and describe how purchased devices function.
A technician cannot reliably replace a missing voltage specification through skill or ingenuity alone.
Diagnostic guesswork caused by missing specifications increases repair time and can damage equipment.
The costs caused by withheld service information fall more heavily on small repair shops than on larger repair organizations.
Large service networks can distribute diagnostic-subscription, specialized-equipment, and training expenses across many locations.
Independent repair operations generally have fewer repairs over which to recover diagnostic-subscription, equipment, and training charges than large service networks do.
Uncertainty about labor and the possibility of a second teardown makes shops less able to offer repairs at prices customers will accept.
Some economically or technically viable repair jobs are not accepted because of the costs or uncertainty created by unavailable service information.
Access to documentation determines whether replacement parts are usable in at least some repairs.
Some devices reject physically compatible replacement parts, limit their functions, or display persistent warnings because of parts-pairing controls.
Manufacturers and large service chains hold advantages over independent repair shops that a service-information disclosure rule would not eliminate.
Providing the proposed disclosures would improve independent shops' ability to compete on skill, price, and service.
Manufacturers or authorized service organizations possess privileged access to repair information or tools unavailable to independent shops.
